```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
```

## Problem 1

```{r load-noaa}
data("ny_noaa")

colSums(is.na(ny_noaa))
```

The data have `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns from
`r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` New York stations from 1981 to 2010. Each row is
one station on one day, with its ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow
depth, and high and low temperatures. About 44% of temperatures are missing,
so this is a major issue. Missing values also make up 6% of precipitation,
15% of snowfall, and 23% of snow depth.

### Data cleaning

```{r clean-noaa}
noaa_df = ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"),
           sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5)
```

Temperatures are in C, and precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth are in mm.
The most common snowfall values are 0, 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm. Zero is most
common because most days have no snow. The other values may come from
converting half or whole inches to mm.

### January and July temperatures

```{r monthly-temperature, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5}
temp_df = noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax)) |>
  mutate(month = if_else(month == 1, "January", "July"))

ggplot(temp_df, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (C)"
  )
```

July is warmer than January, and January changes more across years. Most
stations show similar changes, but one station has a much lower July
average of about 14 C in 1988.

### Temperature and snowfall distributions

```{r temperature-snowfall, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 9}
temp_plot = noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    x = "Minimum temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snow_plot = noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))

temp_plot / snow_plot
```

As tmin rises, tmax usually rises too. For snowfall between 0 and 100 mm,
the yearly patterns look similar, and each year's median is 25 mm.

## Problem 2

```{r clean-nhanes}
covar_df = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4,
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  drop_na() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  mutate(
    SEQN = as.character(SEQN),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent",
                 "More than high school")
    )
  )

accel_df = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(SEQN = as.character(SEQN)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute),
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

nhanes_df = inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "SEQN")
```

```{r education-table}
covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Male", "Female"))
```

```{r age-distribution, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(covar_df, aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Age (years)")
```

The largest group has more than high school education. Men and women have
similar counts in the lowest and highest groups, but the high school group
has more men. People in the highest group tend to be younger, while women
in the high school group tend to be older than men.

```{r total-activity, message = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4}
total_df = nhanes_df |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarise(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(total_df, aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Older adults tend to have lower total activity, but this pattern is weaker
in the highest education group. Women also tend to have higher totals than
men in the two higher education groups.


```{r daily-activity, message = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4}
daily_df = nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, hour) |>
  summarise(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(daily_df, aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.2, se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  labs(
    x = "Hour",
    y = "Mean activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Activity is low at night, rises in the morning, and falls in the evening.
Women tend to have higher daytime activity in the two higher education
groups, while men and women are closer in the lowest group.

## Problem 3

```{r load-citi}
jan2020_df = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july2020_df = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan2024_df = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july2024_df = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

citi_df = bind_rows(jan2020_df, july2020_df, jan2024_df, july2024_df) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                 "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"),
      labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic", "Electric")
    )
  )
```

After adding year and month, the data have `r nrow(citi_df)` rides and
`r ncol(citi_df)` variables. Each row is one ride, with its ID, bike type,
weekday, duration in minutes, stations, and membership status. These are
1% samples of rides under 4 hours from January and July in 2020 and 2024,
and some station names are missing.

```{r citi-counts}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member"))
```

Members have more rides in each month, and both groups have more rides in
July than January. Counts are also higher in 2024 than in 2020.

```{r citi-stations}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July", !is.na(start_station_name)) |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Starting station", "Rides"))
```

```{r citi-median-duration, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
median_df = citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(median_df,
       aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    x = "Day",
    y = "Median duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  )
```

Median duration is higher in July than January and in 2020 than 2024.
It is also usually higher on weekends, but not on Sunday in January 2024.

```{r citi-duration-2024, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    x = "Rider type",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes, log scale)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )
```

Casual riders tend to have longer trips, and trips are longer in July.
Electric trips tend to be shorter for casual riders but slightly longer
for members. All groups have a few very long trips.
